title: How to Make Good Habits Inevitable and Bad Habits Impossible
hook: Hand the phone to your roommate at 10pm with a note that says do not return it until 7am, no matter what I say.
counterintuition: Most readers think self-control is a skill you sharpen. It is closer to a budget you spend, and the people who look disciplined are mostly the ones who arranged, hours or weeks earlier, for the hard choice to no longer be theirs to make.
tryThisNow: Pick one habit you most want to break. Delete the app, move the object, or lock the door. Do one right now. The choice is locked the moment you finish.
keyTakeaway: You will not out-argue your tired self at the worst hour, so close the door at the best one: build the friction in advance, while calm, and let the small barrier hold.

breakdown.fastRead: At 9:58 pm, a night-shift nurse hands her phone to her roommate with one rule: do not return it until 7 am, no matter what I say. By 1 am she would have been on TikTok. She isn't. The phone is in another room and the roommate is asleep. That is a commitment device. You lock the choice in now, while you still want the right thing, so the tired you at 1 am does not get a vote. Decide once, while you are clear. The bad move should be impossible by the time it tempts you, not after.
breakdown.deepRead:
An orchestra teacher swore off weekend email for a year and broke the rule by 10 am every Saturday. Then he tried something duller. Every Friday at 5 pm, he deletes the mail app from his phone. To check email Saturday, he has to redownload it, sign in, approve two codes. He never does. Saturday survives, not because he got stronger, but because he made the wrong move annoying.

This is the small idea inside a big one. You will not out-argue your tired self at 11 pm or 3 pm or Saturday morning. That version of you is not lazy. He is running on fumes, and fumes lose to a pantry door six feet away. So you do not negotiate with him. You take the choice away in advance, while you are calm, and you make the path to defection slightly stupid.

A freelance illustrator tapes her pantry shut with painter's tape each morning. At 3 pm she stands there and considers peeling it. She doesn't. Peeling tape feels embarrassing in a way that opening a cupboard does not. The barrier is laughable on paper. That is exactly why it works. The cost is not muscular, it is social and a little silly, and the cookies stay in the bag.

You do not break a habit by trying harder at the worst hour. You break it by closing the door at the best one.
breakdown.fullRead:
A city council aide has been almost-starting a book proposal for three years. He keeps promising himself a 5 am writing hour. He keeps sleeping through it. Last month he did one strange thing: he hired a Saturday writing coach for four hundred dollars a week, prepaid, who only earns the money if he sends pages by Friday. The 5 am hour stopped being a fight with his alarm clock. It became a four-hundred-dollar question, asked in advance, on a Sunday, by a calmer version of him.

That is the move. A commitment device is a decision made by a clear-eyed you on Sunday that binds a tired you on Thursday. You set the trap when the prey is not in the room.

Willpower is real, but it runs out. Treat it like a small daily allowance that gets spent by lunch and is gone by the time the cookies start whispering. If you keep designing systems that assume the 11 pm version of you will hold the line, you are designing for a person who does not exist after dinner.

A partner at a small law firm has resolved every January for nine years to leave by 6 pm. She never does. Last spring she had a quiet, awkward conversation with her office manager: please lock my office at 6:01 pm. Please refuse to reopen it, even if I ask. The hardest part was not the rule. It was handing over authority she would not exercise on herself. That handoff is the whole mechanism. The lock is just hardware. The real device is the agreement, and the cost of breaking it is asking another adult to break it for you.

Not every device survives a bad day. A recovering gambler can promise himself a different route home, and on most Tuesdays that promise holds. But on a bad Tuesday, the kind where a client yelled and the train was late and his daughter texted something cold, the route becomes a choice again. One slip and a year of savings, a marriage, a custody arrangement can move in an evening. Compare that to a route his phone navigates for him, with the parlor's address blocked in his maps. One device costs nothing and survives good days. The other costs a little and survives bad ones. The right question is never which device is clever. It is which device still works on the worst version of the day you are likely to have.

Three tests for a real device. First, does it bind in advance, before the wanting starts? Second, does it move the cost of defection from your willpower to something outside you: a roommate, a deleted app, a prepaid coach, a locked door? Third, would it still hold if the tired, hungry, angry version of you wanted to override it? If the answer to any of those is no, you have a resolution, not a device.

You are not one person across a week. You are a committee that meets in shifts, and only the Sunday morning shift writes the rules. Your job is to make those rules load-bearing by the time Thursday night arrives. Tape the pantry. Hand over the phone. Pay the coach. Give someone else the key. The bad habit does not lose at 11 pm. It loses on Sunday, when you make 11 pm a decision you no longer get to make.

examples.title: Saskue hands her phone to her roommate at ten

planSpec.domain: a pediatric night-shift nurse who keeps scrolling TikTok until 4am on her days off and wrecking her sleep cycle
planSpec.audience: a shift worker whose schedule already fights them
planSpec.stakes: whether she shows up to a 12-hour shift with the cognition of a drunk driver
planSpec.requiredBeat: she physically hands her phone to her roommate at 10pm with a written note saying 'do not return until 7am no matter what I say', and the doc shows the moment she would have caved if the option were still hers

examples.scenario: It is 9:57pm on a Sunday. Saskue is off until Tuesday night, and her phone is already warm in her palm, three TikToks deep. She works pediatric nights, and the last time she scrolled until 4am she missed a saline calculation on a six-year-old and a charge nurse caught it. Her roommate is in the kitchen. On the counter sits a sticky note in Saskue's handwriting: do not return until 7am no matter what I say. Her thumb finds a new video. She can feel the version of herself at 1am who will text the roommate, just for the alarm, promise. Her hand hovers above the counter, phone face down on the note.
examples.whatToDo: Walk to the kitchen now and hand the phone and the note to the roommate. Say it out loud. Do not negotiate terms; the 10pm Saskue is the only one who gets a vote.
examples.whyItMatters: The 1am version of her wants the phone back and will out-argue the 10pm version every time. Moving the phone out of reach moves the decision out of the hands of the weakest decider.

examples.title: Gareth deletes the mail icon at five on Friday

planSpec.domain: a high school orchestra teacher trying to stop checking work email on weekends
planSpec.audience: a salaried professional with no enforced boundaries
planSpec.stakes: a marriage that is quietly running on fumes because Saturday is never actually Saturday
planSpec.requiredBeat: before: he white-knuckles a 'no email Saturday' rule and fails by 10am; after: he deletes the mail app from his phone every Friday at 5pm and the friction is enough that Saturday survives

examples.scenario: Before: Gareth, the orchestra teacher at Northfield High, declares a no-email rule on a Friday night and lasts until 10:02 the next morning, when he thumbs the inbox 'just to scan,' finds a parent complaint about chair placement, and spends the rest of the day half-present at his daughter's recital. After: the following Friday at 5pm he stands in the school parking lot and long-presses the mail icon until it wobbles, then taps delete. By Saturday morning the urge arrives, but the icon is gone. Reinstalling means signing in, finding the password, waiting on two-factor.
examples.whatToDo: Each Friday at 5pm, delete the mail app from your phone. Reinstall Monday morning at school. Let the reinstall friction be the rule, not your resolve.
examples.whyItMatters: Saturday-morning Gareth has less self-control than Friday-evening Gareth. The deletion is a decision made by the stronger version of him that the weaker version cannot quietly reverse.

examples.title: Iolanthe Tapes the Pantry Shut at Her Kitchen Table

planSpec.domain: a freelance illustrator who keeps eating an entire sleeve of cookies while drawing at her kitchen table
planSpec.audience: someone who works from home with the pantry six feet away
planSpec.stakes: a creeping pre-diabetic A1C her doctor flagged in March
planSpec.requiredBeat: she narrates the small physical act of taping the pantry shut with painter's tape every morning, and the moment at 3pm when she stands in front of it, considers peeling the tape, and walks away because peeling tape feels stupid in a way that opening a cupboard does not

examples.scenario: Iolanthe inks panels at her kitchen table, six feet from a pantry that holds a sleeve of shortbread. Every morning at 8am she runs a strip of blue painter's tape across the pantry door before she opens her sketchbook. At 3pm the line in panel four refuses to land. She stands up, walks over, and considers peeling the tape. Her thumb finds the edge. Peeling tape, in the kitchen, alone, in daylight, feels stupid in a way that opening a cupboard never did. She walks back to the table.
examples.whatToDo: Add one tiny physical step between the craving and the food. Tape the pantry shut each morning so the 3pm version of you has to perform an absurd act to defect.
examples.whyItMatters: The 3pm self has the weakest judgment and the loudest craving. A commitment device installed by the 8am self shifts the decision to when judgment was strong, and adds friction that shame, not willpower, enforces.

examples.title: Desmond's 5am Hour and the Coach Who Only Cashes On Pages

planSpec.domain: a city council aide trying to write a book proposal in the 5am hour before work
planSpec.audience: someone with one fragile pocket of time and no slack
planSpec.stakes: a manuscript that has been 'almost started' for three years
planSpec.requiredBeat: the reader is asked what single commitment device would make tomorrow's 5am writing inevitable; the reveal shows the aide pre-paying a Saturday writing coach $400/week who only gets paid if he sends pages by Friday — a stake he cannot quietly renegotiate with himself

examples.scenario: Picture Desmond, a city council aide whose book proposal has been 'almost started' since 2023. His alarm is set for 4:55am. His laptop is on the kitchen counter, charged. He has done this setup ninety times. By Tuesday of any given week, the 5am hour belongs to email, the snooze button, or a long shower. Before you read on, predict: what one commitment device, set up today, would make tomorrow's 5am writing actually happen? Not motivation. Not a new journal. A mechanism.
examples.whatToDo: Pre-pay a Saturday writing coach $400 a week in advance, on the standing condition that the money is only earned if you email pages by Friday at 5pm.
examples.whyItMatters: The stake has to be one you cannot quietly renegotiate with yourself at 4:55am. Sunk money owed to another human survives a bad Tuesday. A private rule does not.

examples.title: Rashad's commute past the OTB parlor he cannot unsee

planSpec.domain: a recovering gambler who still drives past the off-track betting parlor on his commute home
planSpec.audience: someone for whom one slip costs more than a slip should
planSpec.stakes: eighteen months of recovery and a daughter who just started trusting him again
planSpec.requiredBeat: the reader is asked to design two commitment devices, one that costs nothing and one that costs real money, that would make the next slip mechanically harder; the doc must compare which one would survive a bad Tuesday and why

examples.scenario: Rashad has eighteen months clean. Every weekday at 6:12pm his commute carries him past the off-track betting parlor on Linden Avenue, and every weekday at 6:12pm his hands tighten on the wheel. His sponsor asked him a question last Tuesday that he has not been able to put down. Suppose you had to design two locks on this commute, one that costs you nothing and one that costs you real money. Which lock would still be holding on a bad Tuesday, the kind of Tuesday where his daughter is at her mother's and the apartment is quiet?
examples.whatToDo: Sketch both devices. Free: reroute the GPS to a longer street that does not pass Linden. Paid: hand your debit card to your sister Mondays, retrieve it Fridays. Pick the one a bad Tuesday cannot undo.
examples.whyItMatters: The free device works on a normal day and dissolves on a hard one, because the steering wheel still belongs to you. The paid device removes the mechanism of the slip itself. Cost is not the point. Irrevocability is.

examples.title: Rhoswen asks her office manager to lock the door at 6:01pm

planSpec.domain: a partner at a small law firm who promises every January to leave the office by 6pm and never does
planSpec.audience: a senior professional whose calendar is the problem
planSpec.stakes: a back that has begun to spasm and a teenager who has stopped asking about dinner
planSpec.requiredBeat: a conversation with her office manager in which she asks him to lock her office at 6:01pm and refuse to reopen it; the dialogue lands on the discomfort of giving someone else the authority she will not exercise on herself, and why that transfer is the whole mechanism

examples.scenario: Rhoswen catches her office manager, Davies, in the hallway on a Tuesday and shuts the door behind him. 'I want you to lock my office at 6:01pm every weekday,' she says. 'And refuse to reopen it. No matter what I say.' Davies blinks. 'Even if you tell me it's urgent?' 'Especially then.' He folds his arms. 'Why me? You own the firm.' 'Because at 5:58 I will want one more email, and I will lose. You won't.' He studies her for a long second. 'You're handing me the authority you won't use on yourself.' 'Yes.' 'That's the whole point, isn't it.'
examples.whatToDo: Hand the lockout key to someone whose 6pm self is not negotiating with your 5:58 self, and make their refusal binding before the craving arrives.
examples.whyItMatters: Willpower is lowest at the moment of defection. A device held by another person converts a daily ego contest into a door that does not open, which is a fight your tired self cannot have.

questions.prompt: A wedding planner wants to stop replying to client emails after 8pm. She tells herself, 'I just won't open the laptop.' Why does this approach fall short of a real commitment device?
choices: It depends on her future self deciding correctly at the exact moment willpower is lowest, with no added friction.
It is too vague because it does not specify which clients are off limits.
It does not include a measurable target, so she cannot tell if she succeeded.
questions.explanation: A commitment device removes the option to defect; a rule only states the intention. Specificity and measurability are useful, but neither helps when 9pm arrives and the laptop is still within easy reach.

questions.prompt: A line cook finishes a closing shift at 2am. The bar staff routinely offers free beers and he has been trying to stop drinking on work nights. Which move best locks in tomorrow's clear head?
choices: Promise himself he will accept only one beer and head straight home.
Leave his car keys with a coworker who lives nearby and only retrieve them after she clocks out and walks ahead.
Decide in the moment whether the urge feels manageable enough to refuse.
questions.explanation: Handing keys over makes leaving the bar the path of least resistance and ties his ride home to her schedule. The other choices leave the 2am version of him in charge, which is exactly when his judgment is weakest.

questions.prompt: A first-year law student keeps opening Reddit during evening study blocks. She wants the next two hours of focus to actually happen. What is the soundest setup?
choices: Install a site blocker, hand the unlock password to her partner before each session, and set it to lift at 10pm.
Set a 20-minute focus timer and try to power through the urges as they come.
Tell herself she will close the tab the moment she notices she opened it.
questions.explanation: Giving the password away removes her ability to override the block when the urge spikes. Timers and self-noticing both rely on the same version of her who already lost this fight last night, so the design does no real work.

questions.prompt: A retired engineer wants to attend his Tuesday tai chi class, but as soon as it rains he convinces himself to skip. What single change makes next Tuesday most likely to happen?
choices: Set a reminder alarm one hour before class and re-read the weekly schedule.
Pre-pay the full semester as non-refundable and arrange a carpool with a neighbor who is counting on the ride.
Promise himself he will make up any skipped class on Thursday morning.
questions.explanation: The sunk fee plus the neighbor's expectation make skipping cost something concrete in the same week. A reminder leaves the choice intact, and a 'make it up later' rule lets him quietly renegotiate the commitment with himself.

questions.prompt: A graphic designer's father, newly pre-diabetic, has tried to walk 30 minutes each morning for a month. The couch usually wins. Which plan locks tomorrow's walk in place?
choices: Lay out walking shoes by the door and set the coffee maker on a timer.
Read an article each night about the benefits of walking for blood sugar.
Schedule a 7am walk with a neighbor who knocks on the door, plus a commitment app that donates $20 to a cause he opposes for each missed walk.
questions.explanation: The knock at the door and the automatic penalty remove the choice from his groggy 7am self. Shoes by the door is friction reduction that he can override, and reading reasons is willpower-by-information, which fades by morning.

questions.prompt: A novelist asks her sister to delete Twitter from her phone every Sunday night and reinstall it Friday after work. Why is this design stronger than a personal 'no Twitter on weekdays' rule?
choices: It moves enforcement to her sister, so the weekday version of her cannot quietly defect.
It involves a family member, which adds emotional accountability.
It limits Twitter to weekends, which is a more balanced schedule overall.
questions.explanation: The mechanism is that her future self never gets to make the call. Emotional accountability is real but renegotiable, and 'balance' is a side effect, not the lever. The transfer of authority is what makes the rule hold.

questions.prompt: A small business owner pairs two strategies to stop ordering Friday pizza: (1) hide delivery apps in a folder named 'boring', and (2) hand her credit card to a friend from Thursday to Sunday. Which is doing more of the work, and why?
choices: (1), because reducing visual cues is the foundation of habit redesign.
(2), because it physically removes the means to defect; (1) is friction she can still bypass in 30 seconds.
They are equivalent, since both raise the cost of ordering pizza.
questions.explanation: Hiding apps is a soft cue change she can undo with a swipe. Handing the card away means even a fully decided 9pm version of her cannot complete the order. The strength of a device is whether it survives the worst moment of the week.

questions.prompt: A music producer signs a contract: if he misses a 9am studio session, his manager wires $500 to a cause he loathes. Two months in, he has missed zero sessions. What is the contract actually doing?
choices: Creating fear of social embarrassment among industry peers.
Reminding him each morning that he made a public commitment.
Removing his ability to defect cheaply, because the penalty is pre-set and his 8:45am self has no way to cancel it.
questions.explanation: The penalty is locked in before the moment of weakness, and the recipient is picked to make defection psychologically painful. Reminders and social pressure can help, but the binding mechanism here is what makes the rule self-enforcing.

questions.prompt: A bike commuter wants to stop snoozing his 5:30am alarm so he can actually ride to work. He is weighing three approaches. Which is the most defensible choice?
choices: Move the alarm clock across the bedroom so he has to stand up to silence it.
Ask his partner to refuse to speak to him in the morning until he is out of bed.
Sign up for a non-refundable 6am cycling class and arrange to meet a friend at the corner who waits five minutes, then leaves.
questions.explanation: The class fee and the waiting friend make skipping cost something real and immediate that his 5:30am self cannot wave away. Crossing the room is easy to defeat by going back to bed, and conscripting his partner makes her the enforcer of his habit.

reviewCards.front: You know you will scroll your phone in bed at midnight no matter what promises you make at noon. What single move does this call for?
reviewCards.back: Build a commitment device today that removes the option later. Hand the phone to a roommate at 10pm with a written note saying do not return it until morning. The point is to lock the choice in now, when willpower is highest, so the late-night you cannot defect.

reviewCards.front: A teacher swears off weekend work email every Friday, then caves by 10am Saturday. What concrete change would actually hold the line?
reviewCards.back: Add friction the future self cannot quietly skip. Delete the mail app from the phone every Friday at 5pm, so opening email on Saturday requires reinstalling, signing in, and waiting. The fix is not more resolve, it is making the defect path mechanically annoying.

reviewCards.front: You want to write at 5am tomorrow and you have wanted to for three years. Design one commitment device that makes tomorrow inevitable.
reviewCards.back: Put money and another person between you and quitting. Pre-pay a coach a real sum each week, payable only if you send pages by Friday. A stake you cannot renegotiate with yourself at 4:55am is what turns a fragile intention into a fixed appointment.

reviewCards.front: A recovering gambler still drives past the betting parlor every evening. Compare a free commitment device with one that costs real money: which survives a bad Tuesday?
reviewCards.back: Both can work, but rank them by what a tired, rationalizing self can undo. Rerouting the drive is free and strong if the new route is the default GPS path. A bank account with a trusted co-signer on withdrawals costs money but resists the 4pm bargaining voice better, because undoing it requires another human.

reviewCards.front: You keep promising to leave the office by 6pm and never do. What is the move, in one line?
reviewCards.back: Lock the choice in advance by giving someone else control of the exit. Have an assistant put a non-movable 6pm calendar block with a named obligation outside the building, recurring daily, that you cannot reschedule yourself. The decision happens once, not every evening at 5:55.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is pre-commitment: deciding once, when you are clearheaded, what your tired self will be forced to do later. Practiced enough, you stop trusting in-the-moment willpower and start engineering the moment so the wrong choice is mechanically harder than the right one. You become someone who hands the keys to a future-proof system, not someone who hopes to feel strong at 10pm.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you find yourself checking work email after hours more than twice in a week, then delete the mail app from your phone every Friday at 5pm and reinstall it Monday morning.
If you keep grazing on the same snack while you work, then put a strip of painter's tape across the pantry or drawer each morning so opening it requires a deliberate two-step act, not a reflex.
If a personal project keeps slipping for months, then pre-pay a coach or accountability partner a real sum each week that only releases when you send the work by a fixed deadline.
If you cannot trust yourself to stop scrolling at night, then hand your phone to someone else at a set time with a written note telling them not to return it until morning no matter what you say.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick the one habit you have failed at most this year and write down a single commitment device you can set up before bed tonight, app deleted, phone handed over, money on the line, or door locked by someone else. Put it in place before you sleep, even if the version is clumsy.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Every Sunday, run a ten-minute audit of the week ahead and ask which one decision your tired self is most likely to botch. Build one commitment device for that specific moment, something physical or financial that another person controls, and put it in place before Monday starts.

memorableLines.text: A commitment device is a decision made by a clear-eyed you on Sunday that binds a tired you on Thursday. You set the trap when the prey is not in the room.
memorableLines.why: Distills the entire chapter's mechanism into one definition. The trap metaphor is apt and surprising—it shows that commitment devices work by deciding in advance, when rational, to bind your future self.

memorableLines.text: You are not one person across a week. You are a committee that meets in shifts, and only the Sunday morning shift writes the rules.
memorableLines.why: A single sentence that reframes identity in an unexpected way. It's the psychological insight that explains why willpower fails and justifies why commitment devices are necessary.

memorableLines.text: The barrier is laughable on paper. That is exactly why it works. The cost is not muscular, it is social and a little silly, and the cookies stay in the bag.
memorableLines.why: Captures the counterintuitive core of the chapter: the smallest, silliest barriers are most effective because they work on shame, not strength. The concrete image sticks the abstract principle.
